The escape velocity \(v_e\) from a celestial body is given by  

\[
v_e = \sqrt{\frac{2\mu}{R}},
\]

where  

- \(\mu = 4.282837 \times 10^{13}\ \text{m}^3\!/\text{s}^2\) (gravitational parameter of Mars),  
- \(R = 3.389500 \times 10^{6}\ \text{m}\) (radius of Mars).

**Step 1: Compute the ratio \(\frac{2\mu}{R}\).**  

\[
2\mu = 2 \times 4.282837 \times 10^{13} = 8.565674 \times 10^{13}\ \text{m}^3\!/\text{s}^2.
\]

\[
\frac{2\mu}{R} = \frac{8.565674 \times 10^{13}}{3.389500 \times 10^{6}}
               = 2.527 \times 10^{7}\ \text{m}^2\!/\text{s}^2.
\]

**Step 2: Take the square root.**  

\[
v_e = \sqrt{2.527 \times 10^{7}} \approx 5.03 \times 10^{3}\ \text{m/s}.
\]

Thus, the escape velocity at Mars’ surface is approximately  

\[
\boxed{5027\ \text{m/s}}.
\]

The escape velocity \(v_{\text{escape}}\) from a celestial body is given by  

\[
v_{\text{escape}} = \sqrt{\frac{2\mu}{R}},
\]

where  

- \(\mu = 4.282837 \times 10^{13}\ \text{m}^3\!/\text{s}^2\) (gravitational parameter of Mars),  
- \(R = 3.389500 \times 10^{6}\ \text{m}\) (radius of Mars).

Plugging in the numbers:

\[
\begin{aligned}
v_{\text{escape}} &= \sqrt{\frac{2 \times 4.282837 \times 10^{13}}{3.389500 \times 10^{6}}} \\

&= \sqrt{2.526 \times 10^{7}} \\

\end{aligned}
\]
